To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) rising atmospheric CO2 concentrations will cause droughts in many regions of the globe to become more severe, and (2) the use of metrics that account for plant physiological response to CO2 reduces the severity of droughts in other regions.

plant physiological responses reduce the amount of water stress predicted by common metrics of drought severity, and that this effect is captured by using metrics that are more plant-centric rather than metrics that are more atmosphere-centric.

the water savings experienced by plants under high CO2 concentrations can compensate for much of their increased transpiration demand under warmer temperatures, and that this compensation is reflected in a different spatial pattern of drought stress than that predicted by common drought metrics that do not account for plant responses to CO2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the effects of rising CO2 on the water balance of the Earth, and the implications of these changes on drought.
the question of how the Earth will respond to the increase in greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere.
the impact of climate change on the water cycle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of CO2 on stomatal conductance, transpiration, and water use efficiency will mitigate the impact of climate warming on drought, but that these effects will vary spatially.
rising CO2 will make drought more severe in some regions and will reduce drought stress in others.

the use of P-E, a measure that represents water available to downstream ecosystems, and soil moisture from Earth system models, reduces the area of the globe that is predicted to become more drought-stressed by climate change, relative to the use of the atmosphere-centric Palmer Drough Severity Index.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of plant-centric metrics in climate change impact analysis reduces uncertainties and leads to different conclusions.
plant responses to CO2 will make droughts less severe in many areas, and this effect is not captured by the most commonly used drought metrics, which are based on precipitation and temperature.
the use of plant-centric drought metrics, such as P-E, can reduce the uncertainty in drought predictions by accounting for both the radiative and physiological effects of increasing CO2.
